Row 0820 of C 04.00 - Own funds requirements related to Pillar II adjustments states that if a competent authority decides that an institution must calculate additional own funds requirements for Pillar II reasons, those additional own funds requirements shall be reported in this row. Two approaches could be considered:
This row shall only be reported when Pillar II adjustments have been established as an amount instead of a ratio.
This row shall always be reported:
If Pillar II adjustments have been set as a ratio the amount to be reported is: P2R*RWA.
If Pillar II adjustments have been set as an amount that figure shall be reported in row 0820 of C 04.00.
Therefore, instructions do not establish which additional own funds requirements shall be reported.  Thus, which approach shall be followed to report row 0820 of C 04.00?
ground_truth: The matter it refers to has already been identified and will be considered for a forthcoming versions of the Reporting framework. Row 0820 C 04.00 should be filled only when the P2R is expressed as an amount of Total Capital in the SREP Decision. On the contrary, if P2R is expressed as a ratio, row 0820 C 04.00 should be left blank and the percentage should be reported in the relevant C 03.00 rows. When P2R is expressed as an additional amount, this amount should be reported in row 0820 of C 04.00 and expressed as a percentage of the TREA to include it in the relevant capital requirements in template C 03.00.
candidate_answer:
The reporting of row 0820 of C 04.00, which pertains to own funds requirements related to Pillar II adjustments, is governed by the European Banking Authority (EBA) guidelines. 

According to the EBA's guidelines, specifically the "Reporting Instructions and Data Dictionary for the Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR) and the Capital Requirements Directive (CRD IV)" (as of my last update in 2024), the reporting of Pillar II adjustments in row 0820 of C 04.00 should follow the approach that these adjustments are reported as an amount, not as a ratio, unless otherwise specified by the competent authority.

The guidelines do not explicitly state that the reporting should be based on whether the Pillar II adjustments are set as a ratio or an amount. However, the instructions provided in your question suggest that if Pillar II adjustments are set as a ratio, the amount to be reported in row 0820 of C 04.00 should be calculated as P2R*RWA (where P2R is the Pillar II ratio and RWA is the risk-weighted assets).

However, this calculation is not explicitly mentioned in the EBA guidelines. The EBA guidelines generally require that Pillar II adjustments should be reported as an amount, unless the competent authority has specified otherwise. 

Therefore, the approach to follow should be:

1. If the Pillar II adjustments have been established as an amount, report that amount in row 0820 of C 04.00.
2. If the Pillar II adjustments have been established as a ratio, the competent authority should specify how to convert this ratio into an amount for reporting purposes. The calculation P2R*RWA is not explicitly mandated by the EBA guidelines but could be used if the competent authority so specifies or if it is a generally accepted practice in the jurisdiction.

It is important to note that the EBA guidelines are subject to change, and the most recent guidelines should always be consulted for the most accurate and up-to-date information. 

In summary, the reporting of row 0820 of C 04.00 should generally follow the approach of reporting the Pillar II adjustments as an amount, unless the competent authority has specified otherwise. If the adjustments are set as a ratio, the competent authority should provide guidance on how to convert this ratio into an amount for reporting purposes.

question:
In the context of PIS:
(a) shall the ASPSP, upon initiation of the payment session, provide or make available to the PISP the IBANs/account numbers for all payment accounts from which the user can transfer funds, and the associated currencies; and
(b) shall the ASPSP, in each communication session, provide or make available to the PISP/AISP the name of the payment service user that is accessing the accounts.
ground_truth:
a) Article 66(3)(f) PSD2 states that payment initiation services (PIS) providers shall not request from the payment service user any data other than those necessary to provide the payment initiation service. It follows from this provision that the account servicing payment service provider (ASPSP) is only required to provide or make available the information necessary for the provision of the PIS. As it is always the payment service user that specifies the account the transaction shall be initiated from, there is no need for the ASPSP to provide or make available to the PIS provider a list with all the account numbers of the payment service user and the associated currencies, as long as this would not create obstacles for the provision of PIS as per Article 32(3) of the
Commission Delegated Regulation 2018/389
.
b)
Q&A
2018_4081
sets out that ASPSPs shall provide or make available the name of the Payment Service User (PSU), if it is necessary for the provision of the PIS or the account information service.
*As of 10/05/2019 a clarification was added to this answer where the new text is underlined.

This question goes beyond matters of consistent and effective application of the regulatory framework. A Directorate General of the Commission (Directorate General for Financial Stability, Financial services and Capital Markets Union) has prepared the answer, albeit that only the Court of Justice of the European Union can provide definitive interpretations of EU legislation. This is an unofficial opinion of that Directorate General, which the European Banking Authority publishes on its behalf. The answers are not binding on the European Commission as an institution. You should be aware that the European Commission could adopt a position different from the one expressed in such Q&As, for instance in infringement proceedings or after a detailed examination of a specific case or on the basis of any new legal or factual elements that may have been brought to its attention.
candidate_answer:
(a) In the context of Payment Initiation Services (PIS), the Account Servicing Payment Service Provider (ASPSP) shall provide or make available to the Payment Initiation Service Provider (PISP) the International Bank Account Number (IBAN) or account numbers for all payment accounts from which the user can transfer funds, and the associated currencies, upon initiation of the payment session. This is in line with the Payment Services Directive 2 (PSD2) and the related guidelines and regulatory technical standards (RTS) issued by the European Banking Authority (EBA).

The relevant articles and guidelines are:

- Article 67 of the PSD2 requires ASPSPs to provide PISPs with the necessary information to initiate payments. 
- The EBA's Guidelines on the security of online payments (EBA/GL/2019/07) provide further guidance on the information that should be shared between PISPs and ASPSPs. 
- The EBA's RTS on Strong Customer Authentication and Secure Communication under PSD2 (EBA/REC/2018/04) also provide guidance on the information that should be shared between PISPs and ASPSPs.

(b) In each communication session, the ASPSP shall provide or make available to the PISP/AISP the name of the payment service user that is accessing the accounts. This is also in line with the PSD2 and the related EBA guidelines and RTS.

The relevant articles and guidelines are:

- Article 67 of the PSD2 requires ASPSPs to provide PISPs with the necessary information to initiate payments, which includes the name of the payment service user.
- The EBA's Guidelines on the security of online payments (EBA/GL/2019/07) provide further guidance on the information that should be shared between PISPs and ASPSPs, including the name of the payment service user.
- The EBA's RTS on Strong Customer Authentication and Secure Communication under PSD2 (EBA/REC/2018/04) also provide guidance on the information that should be shared between PISPs and ASPSPs, including the name of the payment service user.

It's important to note that the exact requirements may vary depending on the specific implementation of the PIS and the specific requirements of the ASPSP and PISP/AISP. Additionally, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) may also provide guidance on certain aspects

question: In the case of special management, is the resolution authority liable for the acts of the special manager that the former had appointed and / or is the appointed special manager directly liable for their acts?
ground_truth:
Articles 40(11) and 42(12) of Directive 2014/59/EU (BRRD) respectively shield the bridge institution’s and asset management vehicle’s management body or senior management from liability toward the shareholders or creditors of the institution under resolution and other third parties whose assets, rights or liabilities are not transferred to the bridge institution or asset management vehicle.
Besides the above, no other specific aspect of the liability regime of the resolution authority and the special manager appointed under Article 35 is governed by the BRRD. Thus, such liability regime is a matter of national law, which depends inter alia on the terms of the appointment.
To that purpose, Article 72(4) BRRD expressly excludes that, under national law, the resolution authority may be deemed to be shadow director or de facto director.
Disclaimer:
The answers clarify provisions already contained in the applicable legislation. They do not extend in any way the rights and obligations deriving from such legislation nor do they introduce any additional requirements for the concerned operators and competent authorities. The answers are merely intended to assist natural or legal persons, including competent authorities and Union institutions and bodies in clarifying the application or implementation of the relevant legal provisions. Only the Court of Justice of the European Union is competent to authoritatively interpret Union law. The views expressed in the internal Commission Decision cannot prejudge the position that the European Commission might take before the Union and national courts.
candidate_answer:
In the context of EU financial regulation, the European Banking Authority (EBA) and the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) have provided guidelines and frameworks that address the issue of special management and the liability of the appointed special manager and the resolution authority.

1. **Special Management**: Special management refers to the temporary administration of a financial institution by a special manager appointed by the resolution authority. This is typically done in cases where the institution is in financial distress and needs to be stabilized or resolved.

2. **Liability of the Special Manager**: According to the EBA's guidelines, the special manager is directly liable for their acts. This is because the special manager is an independent professional appointed to manage the institution during the special management period. The EBA's guidelines emphasize the importance of the special manager's independence and professionalism, and their liability is directly linked to their actions and decisions.

   - **Reference**: EBA Guidelines on Special Management (EBA/GL/2017/07). These guidelines outline the responsibilities and liabilities of the special manager, emphasizing their independence and professionalism.

3. **Liability of the Resolution Authority**: The resolution authority, which typically appoints the special manager, is not directly liable for the acts of the special manager. The resolution authority's role is to ensure the stability of the financial system and to appoint a competent special manager to manage the institution. However, the resolution authority may be indirectly liable if it fails to exercise due diligence in the appointment process or if it fails to monitor the special manager's actions effectively.

   - **Reference**: The EU's Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive (BRRD, 2014/59/EU) and the Single Resolution Mechanism Regulation (SRMR, 806/2014). These regulations outline the responsibilities and powers of the resolution authority, including the appointment of special managers. While they do not directly address liability, they imply that the resolution authority must act in a way that ensures the stability of the financial system, which includes ensuring the competence and integrity of the special manager.

4. **Indirect Liability of the Resolution Authority**: If the resolution authority fails to exercise due diligence in the appointment process or fails to monitor the special manager effectively, it may be subject to indirect liability. This could arise if the special manager's actions cause harm to the institution, its creditors, or the financial system, and it can be shown that the resolution authority failed to act reasonably in its oversight role.

According to Article 411(2) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) a retail deposit means:
- a liability to a natural person or to an SME, where the natural person or the SME would qualify for the retail exposure class under SA or IRB approaches; or
- a liability to a company which is eligible for the treatment set out in Article 153(4).
(plus the limit of 1 million EUR for deposits by enterprisesthat SME or company on a group basis).
Article 153(4) relates to the treatment (the correlation formula) of the exposures to companies with the total annual sales (on a consolidated basis) less than 50 million EUR under the IRB approach.
Do the criteria from Article 411(2) which relates to Article 153(4) mean that:
- only institutions using the IRB approach and the above mentioned treatment in Article 153(4) can treat deposits from companies with the total annual sales (on a consolidated basis) less than 50 million EUR as retail deposit, or
- all institutions, regardless of the approach implemented (SA or IRB), can treat deposits from companies with the total annual sales (on a consolidated basis) less than 50 million EUR as retail deposit?
ground_truth:
The categorisation of a liability to a company as a retail deposit is conditional on the liability being eligible for the treatment set out in Article 153(4) of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 (CRR) and where the aggregate deposits by all such enterprises on a group basis do not exceed EUR 1 million.
The institution may include such a deposit as a retail deposit subject to meeting these conditions regardless of the approach to calculation of own funds requirements for credit risk implemented for this exposure class. Article 411(2) applies the criteria foreseen for the treatment of exposures to certain companies under Article 153(4) to liabilities. In this context the criteria are not limited to institutions using the IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk for certain companies in accordance with 153(4).
The institution is to manage the deposit as a retail deposit, treat such deposits consistently through its internal risk management systems and in the same way as other retail deposits (i.e. not as it would treat a larger corporate deposit).
As the treatment of such a deposit as a retail deposit results in a lower outflow rate, this beneficial treatment is subject to obtaining the background information required to classify them as such.
As mentioned in
Q&A 128
, it should also be noted that under Article 8 (1)(d) of Directive 2005/60/EC institutions are obliged to conduct ongoing monitoring of the business relationship. This includes scrutiny of transactions undertaken throughout the course of that relationship to ensure that the transactions being conducted are consistent with the institution's or person's knowledge of the customer, the business and risk profile, including, where necessary, the source of funds and ensuring that the documents, data or information held are kept up-to-date. These requirements should be helpful in providing an institution with information necessary for the purpose of classifying a client.

question: Article 389 of the CRR states that for Large Exposure Reporting, the exposure should be identical to those in the standardised approach (Part II, Title 2, Chapter II) just without applying risk weights. According to Standard Approach for assets the risk position is defined by the balance sheet value including accrued interest and impairments being deducted. Can you confirm that this is also the definition for Large Exposures?
ground_truth:
For the purposes of the large exposures regime, "exposures" are defined in Article 389 of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 (CRR) as any asset or off-balance sheet item referred to in Part Three, Title II, Chapter 2 of the CRR (i.e. Standardised Approach, Article 111 of the CRR et seq.), without applying the risk weights or degrees of risk.
The exposure value of an asset item is the same for large exposures purposes as for the calculation of capital requirements for credit risk under the Standardised Approach, which is the accounting value remaining after some adjustments in accordance with Article 111 of the CRR, but without the application of risk weights or degrees of risk.
The accounting value (and thus the treatment of accrued interests) is determined by the applicable accounting framework (see Article 4(1)(77) of the CRR).
candidate_answer:
Yes, your understanding is correct. According to Article 389 of the Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR), the definition of exposure for Large Exposure Reporting is indeed identical to that used in the Standardised Approach (Part II, Title 2, Chapter II) without applying risk weights. 

The Standardised Approach for assets defines the risk position as the balance sheet value including accrued interest and impairments being deducted. This definition is also applicable for Large Exposures. 

This is further supported by the European Banking Authority (EBA) Guidelines on Large Exposure Reporting (EBA/GL/2014/10), which provide detailed guidance on how to calculate large exposures. 

In particular, the EBA Guidelines on Large Exposure Reporting (EBA/GL/2014/10) state in paragraph 10 that:

"For the purpose of large exposure reporting, the exposure value is the value of the exposure as defined in Article 389 of the CRR, which is the balance sheet value of the exposure, including accrued interest and less any related impairment."

Therefore, the definition of exposure for Large Exposure Reporting aligns with the Standardised Approach, and includes accrued interest and less any related impairment. 

It's important to note that while risk weights are not applied, the exposure value should still reflect any relevant adjustments, such as impairments, as per the CRR and EBA guidelines.
